key_points.point: The document asserts that recursive self-improvement, where AI systems autonomously design and develop their successors, is a plausible future trajectory. It notes that while not inevitable, the trend of delegating development tasks to AI is accelerating. This matters to accelerationists because it represents the potential for an intelligence explosion that could rapidly solve complex scientific and societal problems. The document acknowledges that this capability is not yet fully realized and depends on continued compute and architectural progress.
key_points.verbatim: Taken far enough, and given enough compute, that trend points to an AI system capable of fully autonomously designing and developing its own successor. This is called recursive self-improvement.

key_points.point: The document champions AI as a transformative force for global progress in science, healthcare, and other critical domains. It argues that automating the 'perspiration' of research allows for faster experimentation and discovery. From an accelerationist perspective, this validates the strategy of scaling compute and tools to maximize output. The document notes that even if research 'taste' remains a human bottleneck, the compounding efficiency gains are significant.
key_points.verbatim: AI that can build itself would be a major development in the history of technology—one that could bring enormous good for the world in science, healthcare, and beyond.

key_points.point: The document frames AI-driven automation as a massive productivity multiplier that allows smaller teams to achieve the output of much larger organizations. It cites internal data showing Anthropic engineers shipping 8x more code per quarter compared to previous years. This supports the accelerationist view that AI acts as a positive supply shock, lowering costs and expanding output. The document caveats that lines of code are an imperfect metric, but subjective employee polls confirm significant productivity gains.
key_points.verbatim: In the second quarter of 2026, the typical engineer was merging 8x as much code per day as they were in 2024. This is because much of the code is written by Claude, with the engineer directing and reviewing, rather than typing it themselves.

key_points.point: The document advocates for the deployment of autonomous agents that can run code and delegate tasks to other agents to streamline operations. It highlights that agents have moved from simple code generation to running experiments and managing complex research loops. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of building an agentic enterprise backbone to drive innovation. The document notes that human roles are shifting toward oversight and direction-setting as these agents become more capable.
key_points.verbatim: Agents can now run code themselves and delegate hours of work to other agents.

key_points.point: The document observes that AI models are increasingly capable of performing open-ended research tasks, such as proposing hypotheses and iterating on experiments. It cites a demonstration where agents recovered 97% of a performance gap in an AI safety problem, compared to 23% by human researchers. This supports the accelerationist belief that AI can acquire and disseminate cognitive abilities that enhance human-led research. The document acknowledges that humans still choose the problems and scoring rubrics.
key_points.verbatim: Claude-powered agents were given an open problem in AI safety—roughly, can a weaker model reliably supervise a stronger one?—and were left to solve it.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the use of empirical benchmarks and internal data to measure AI progress and safety. It argues that observable performance on real-world tasks is the best indicator of capability. This aligns with the accelerationist preference for empirical, output-based safety verification. The document notes that benchmarks like SWE-bench and CORE-bench have been saturated, indicating rapid progress.
key_points.verbatim: Public benchmarks say a lot about the capabilities of these systems. But they can’t reveal the impact AI systems are having on speeding up AI development itself. For that, we need direct evidence from within AI companies like Anthropic.

key_points.point: The document prioritizes the rapid development of AI capabilities, noting that the rate of improvement is accelerating. It suggests that doubling task completion lengths every four months is a trend that could lead to weeks-long task completion by 2027. This supports the accelerationist desire to push the frontier of AI capabilities as quickly as possible. The document acknowledges that this pace creates challenges for societal adaptation.
key_points.verbatim: The rate at which AI models improve is accelerating. The length of tasks that they can reliably complete on their own has been doubling roughly every four months, up from an earlier trend of doubling every seven months.

key_points.point: The document proposes that humans should shift their focus to reviewing AI-generated work and setting research directions. It argues that this partnership allows for greater organizational efficiency and faster innovation. This aligns with the accelerationist view of AI as a tool for human and organizational augmentation. The document notes that human review is becoming a new bottleneck as AI generation speed increases.
key_points.verbatim: Once human- and AI-authored code quality reach parity, humans will stop writing code entirely, and shift to only reviewing it.
key_points.excerpt_context: What might the future of work at Anthropic look like?

key_points.point: The document suggests that AI can make advanced intelligence universally accessible, supercharging progress across fields. It highlights that even if models don't achieve perfect 'research taste,' the compounding acceleration from automating perspiration is immense. This supports the accelerationist belief in AI-enabled abundance of genius. The document notes that this progress is largely a function of tools and resources.
key_points.verbatim: It’s becoming clear that much of what advances the frontier is automatable; large-scale research progress is mostly a function of tools and resources, which dictate how fast you can run experiments, how many you can run at once, and how quickly you can get results.

key_points.point: The document encourages diverse experimentation and competition, noting that progress is often incremental and driven by scaling. It suggests that the current workflow of scaling, testing, and fixing is what drives the frontier forward. This aligns with the accelerationist strategy of 'letting a thousand AIs bloom' to maximize progress. The document acknowledges that exogenous shocks could slow this process.
key_points.verbatim: In between, most progress is incremental: we scale something up, see what breaks, fix it, and try again. That is exactly the kind of workflow Claude now excels at.

key_points.point: The document highlights the potential for AI to defend against cyber threats, noting that Project Glasswing identified thousands of vulnerabilities in weeks. This supports the accelerationist intention to accelerate defensive AI capabilities to protect against malicious actors. The document notes that the bottleneck in cyber defense has shifted from finding vulnerabilities to patching them.
key_points.verbatim: Project Glasswing is one early sign: in its first weeks, Mythos Preview found more than ten thousand high- and critical-severity software vulnerabilities across the world’s most important systems.

key_points.point: The document warns that full recursive self-improvement could lead to humans losing control over AI systems. It argues that if systems can build their own successors, the methods for monitoring and shaping their behavior become critical. This aligns with the safetyist concern regarding irreversible power concentration and the loss of human agency. The document acknowledges that the alignment problem in this future is highly uncertain.
key_points.verbatim: But full recursive self-improvement also might increase the risks of humans losing control over AI systems. If systems are capable of fully building their own successors, the ways we secure them, monitor them, and shape their behavior all grow much more important.

key_points.point: The document notes that rare occurrences of misalignment in current models could compound as they build their successors, leading to less understood and more frequent failures. This reflects the safetyist concern about instrumental convergence and the difficulty of maintaining alignment during recursive improvement. The document suggests that we may not be able to verify which trendline we are on.
key_points.verbatim: Alternatively, the rare occurrences of misalignment present in today’s models could compound as the models build their successors, growing more frequent but less understood until we lose control of them.

key_points.point: The document advocates for global coordination to enable a credible slowdown or pause in frontier AI development if necessary. It argues that unilateral pauses are insufficient and that international verification regimes are required to prevent bad actors from gaining an advantage. This aligns with the safetyist intention to prioritize safety-gated deployment. The document acknowledges the extreme difficulty of building such verification infrastructure.
key_points.verbatim: We believe it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development to enable societal structures and alignment research to keep up with the advance of the technology.

key_points.point: The document proposes that frontier AI developers should collaborate to build systems that verify whether others have stopped or slowed development. It highlights the challenge of detectability in AI training runs compared to other technologies like missile silos. This supports the safetyist goal of creating robust, verifiable safety frameworks. The document notes that the world lacks the decades of time needed to build such trust.
key_points.verbatim: These systems would enable frontier AI developers to verify that others globally have actually stopped or slowed, and that a bad actor could not use the auspices of a coordinated slowdown to jump ahead in secret.

key_points.point: The document expresses uncertainty about whether current training methods can solve the alignment problem in a future of recursive self-improvement. It suggests that models might be wise enough to halt development, or they might not. This reflects the safetyist concern that we lack reliable methods for ensuring alignment in advanced systems. The document emphasizes the need for more research into these risks.
key_points.verbatim: How the alignment problem gets solved—or not—in this future is something we are least certain about.

key_points.point: The document plans to organize conversations with policymakers and civil society to address the risks of recursive self-improvement and coordination. It argues that people outside AI companies must be involved in this deliberation. This aligns with the safetyist intention to broaden governance and oversight. The document notes that the window for this investigation is currently open.
key_points.verbatim: In the coming months, we will organize conversations where policymakers, researchers, civil society, and other AI companies can help answer some of the questions this piece raises, especially around full recursive self-improvement and how to create better options for coordination and deliberation.

key_points.point: The document warns that a world driven by fast recursive self-improvement could be dominated by self-improving models that eclipse human capabilities. It notes the difficulty of predicting the economic and social consequences if human labor stops being competitive. This supports the safetyist concern about the loss of human control and the potential for catastrophic societal outcomes. The document emphasizes the unpredictability of this future.
key_points.verbatim: By its nature, a world driven by fast recursive self-improvement could become dominated by the self-improving model as its capabilities fully eclipse those of humans and the model proliferates across the broader economy.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that unilateral pauses by a single lab are achievable but accomplish little beyond changing the front-runner. It argues that a meaningful pause requires multiple well-resourced labs in multiple countries to agree to stop under the same conditions. This aligns with the safetyist focus on systemic, global governance frameworks. The document notes that such regimes are difficult to build.
key_points.verbatim: A unilateral pause by one lab, by contrast, is achievable immediately, but accomplishes much less: it would change who the front-runner is, but it would not create the wider deliberative process that is currently missing.

key_points.point: The document notes that even if model development became fully automated, we cannot predict what that would mean for most humans' daily lives. It highlights the collision between recursive intelligence and the world of human relationships and governance. This reflects the safetyist concern about the societal disruption caused by advanced AI. The document suggests that the felt pace of change will still be set by human-centric bottlenecks.
key_points.verbatim: That collision, where recursive intelligence building itself ever faster meets the world of humans, relationships, and governance, is another part of this future we can’t predict.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the need for research into tools that would allow us to understand which trendline we are on. It suggests that we may not be able to build, integrate, and verify these tools in time. This aligns with the safetyist intention to prioritize interpretability and monitoring research. The document notes that this is a critical challenge for safety.
key_points.verbatim: It’s possible that we can’t build, integrate, and verify the tools that we’d need to understand which trendline we are actually on.

key_points.point: The document warns that AI could be turned to harmful ends, such as authoritarian surveillance and influence operations that tailor manipulation to individuals at scale. This supports the safetyist concern about the misuse of advanced AI capabilities. The document notes that organizations using AI would become much more efficient, which could amplify these risks. It emphasizes the need for verification systems.
key_points.verbatim: This would revolutionize knowledge work and government services, but could also be turned to harmful ends, from authoritarian surveillance of whole populations to influence operations that tailor manipulation to each individual and run at a scale no human team could match.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AI progress is often incremental, driven by scaling and fixing, rather than sudden 'eureka' moments. This aligns with the skeptic view of AI as a tool integrated into existing work practices through iterative refinement. The document notes that paradigm-shifting ideas are rare, and most progress happens in the 'perspiration' phase. This supports the skeptic argument against over-hyping AI as a revolutionary force.
key_points.verbatim: But AI is rarely advanced by 'eureka!' moments. There have been a few of these in AI’s recent history, like the Transformer architecture, or mixture-of-experts models, but paradigm-shifting ideas arrive years apart. In between, most progress is incremental: we scale something up, see what breaks, fix it, and try again.

key_points.point: The document notes that even with recursive intelligence, industrial production, social organization, and markets will not change immediately. It argues that more intelligence cannot learn what a drug does over decades or turn a stranger into a friend in a weekend. This supports the skeptic view that AI is a normal technology that operates within existing human-centric constraints. The document emphasizes that human-centric bottlenecks will persist.
key_points.verbatim: More intelligence can’t learn what a drug does over decades of use, can’t hold elections sooner than a constitution dictates, and can’t turn a stranger into an old friend in a weekend.

key_points.point: The document observes that speeding up one part of a process often shifts the bottleneck elsewhere, citing Amdahl's law. It notes that as code production increases, human code review has become a new bottleneck. This aligns with the skeptic view that organizational hurdles and infrastructure constraints are as important as AI capabilities. The document suggests that spotting and fixing these bottlenecks is a key organizational skill.
key_points.verbatim: But speeding up one part of a process often just shifts the bottleneck elsewhere: overall pace is capped by the parts that haven’t sped up. In computing, this is known as Amdahl’s law, and the same logic can apply to organizations.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that large performance gaps persist in Claude's ability to exercise judgment in choosing goals. It notes that humans still play a meaningful role in direction-setting. This supports the skeptic view of a 'jagged' technological frontier where AI excels at structured tasks but struggles with complex, human-centric realities. The document emphasizes that research taste remains a human comparative advantage.
key_points.verbatim: However, large performance gaps persist when it comes to Claude exercising judgement in choosing goals in both engineering and research. That’s the gap between AI today and a future system that could autonomously design its own successor.

key_points.point: The document notes that the felt pace of the future will still be set by human-centric bottlenecks, even if the laboratory upstream runs at the speed of compute. This aligns with the skeptic perspective that AI integration is a gradual process constrained by existing societal structures. The document emphasizes the collision between recursive intelligence and the world of human relationships.
key_points.verbatim: For most people, the felt pace of this future will still be set by the bottlenecks, even if the laboratory upstream runs at the speed of compute.

key_points.point: The document highlights that Anthropic employees are using Claude to do work that wouldn't have happened otherwise, like building exploratory tooling and addressing long-deferred cleanup. This supports the skeptic view that AI is often used for incremental improvements rather than revolutionary shifts. The document notes that humans struggle to hold large amounts of unfamiliar context, which AI helps mitigate.
key_points.verbatim: We also see evidence that people at Anthropic are using Claude to do work that simply wouldn’t have happened otherwise, like building exploratory tooling and addressing long-deferred cleanup.

key_points.point: The document notes that benchmarks often saturate below 100% due to errors in question and answer sets, such as ambiguous problem statements. This aligns with the skeptic view that AI performance metrics can be misleading and do not always reflect real-world capability. The document emphasizes that benchmarks are imperfect measures of progress.
key_points.verbatim: Especially as they shift toward more open-ended formats and more difficult tasks (e.g., Olympiad-level mathematics), benchmarks often saturate below 100% due to errors in the question and answer sets like ambiguous problem statements and unsolvable questions.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that the comparative advantage of humans is still in seeing the bigger picture and thinking beyond the confines of the immediate task. This supports the skeptic view that AI is a tool for specific, structured tasks rather than a replacement for human judgment. The document notes that this is a persistent gap.
key_points.verbatim: The comparative advantage of humans as of right now is still in seeing the bigger picture and thinking beyond the confines of the immediate task.

key_points.point: The document notes that the rate at which organizations can spot and fix bottlenecks may be a skill that improves over time, becoming the most important skill for any organization. This aligns with the skeptic view that organizational adaptation is the primary challenge of AI integration. The document emphasizes that this is a human-centric process.
key_points.verbatim: The rate at which organizations can spot and fix these bottlenecks may be a skill that improves over time, and it may become the most important skill for any organization.

key_points.point: The document notes that the 'gift economy' of small favors between humans is being replaced by AI, which is faster but creates zero debt and loses bids for human collaboration. This supports the skeptic concern about the social and cultural impact of AI on work environments. The document highlights the loss of mutual awareness.
key_points.verbatim: Work (and life) ran on a gift economy of small favors between humans. 'Can you help me get this script running?' [...] each one created a little debt, a little mutual awareness. [Claude is] faster, it creates zero debt, but each of these is a lost bid for human collaboration.
key_points.excerpt_context: What might the future of work at Anthropic look like?

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that developer estimates of AI productivity uplift can be overestimated, as shown by recent research. This aligns with the skeptic view that subjective impressions of AI impact should be treated with caution. The document emphasizes the need for rigorous methodology in assessing productivity gains.
key_points.verbatim: Many respondents may not have thought carefully about how to account for various biases or subtleties in the question definition, and recent research by METR shows that developer estimates of AI productivity uplift can be overestimated.
